blocks.text: Meridian Actuarial Advisors

We are a consulting actuarial practice. Our work is the measurement of long-term promises: the pensions a public retirement system owes its members, the benefits a multiemployer fund has promised to the people who work under its agreements, and the reserves a life insurer holds against the policies it has written. The people responsible for those promises are boards, trustees, and company officers. They need numbers they can stand behind, and they need to know what those numbers rest on. That is the service we set out to provide.
The work
Our practice is organized around three kinds of client. For each of them the work is a regulated opinion, and we perform it under the Actuarial Standards of Practice that apply to it.

items: 1. Public retirement systems. Annual funding valuations, the accounting information a plan and its employers report under GASB Statements No. 67 and No. 68, and experience studies that test the plan's assumptions against what actually happened to its members.

2. Multiemployer benefit funds. Valuations for the board of trustees, the annual certification of the plan's funded status under the Pension Protection Act, and the projections trustees use when they weigh changes to contributions or benefits.

3. Life insurance companies. Reserve valuation, asset adequacy analysis, support for the appointed actuary's opinion and memorandum, and preparation for principle-based reserving, which will change how many companies set reserves on their life business.

blocks.text: Before the numbers

Every assignment starts with an engagement letter. It states what we will measure, for whom, as of what date, and under which standards. We take care over that page. In our experience most disagreements about actuarial work turn out to be disagreements about scope, and a clear letter settles them before they start.

Data come next. We rely on information the client supplies: member census records, asset statements, plan documents, policy files. We do not audit those data. We do review them for reasonableness and consistency, against the prior year and against each other, in the manner ASOP No. 23 describes. Our reports say what we tested, what we found, and what we relied on without testing.
How our reports read

A report from us keeps three things apart. The first is what the data show. The second is what we assumed. The third is what we conclude from both. A reader should be able to find each one without reading the other two. Where a conclusion depends on an assumption, it gets its own paragraph, and the assumption is named in it. We write plainly. A board member who is not an actuary has to be able to follow the reasoning, and the board's counsel will read the same pages closely.
Who you will work with

Robert Lawrence, our Managing Actuary, signs the firm's actuarial opinions. He reviews each assignment when it is scoped and again before anything is released. He is the person to call about scope, about the standards a piece of work falls under, or about a result that needs explaining.

Carol Cooper, our Practice Manager, runs the practice day to day. She prepares engagement letters, keeps the schedule, sends and tracks data requests, and looks after invoicing and the retention of our files. If you are sending us a census file, or have a question about a bill, she is the right first call.
What we intend

We are a young firm. We intend to grow as the work requires, and to add people on the consulting side first, so that the actuary who scopes an assignment can still be the one who reviews it. We also take on reviews of another actuary's work for a board or its counsel. We regard that as part of the same discipline, and we hold it to the same standards.
Beginning an assignment

We suggest a short conversation before anything is put in writing, because it lets us understand the question before we propose a way to answer it. After that conversation we send a note that sets out:

items: 1. what we understand the question to be;
2. the data we would need, and why each item matters;
3. the standards the work would be performed under; and
4. the timetable and the basis of our fee.

blocks.text: Nothing begins until the client has read that note and agreed with it. If our understanding is wrong, that is the place to find out.
Welcome: Jennifer Johnson

Jennifer Johnson has joined us as an Actuarial Associate, and we are glad she is here. She sits in the consulting group, with the actuaries and analysts who carry the valuation work. She reports to Jennifer Vasquez, Consulting Actuary, who will assign her work and review it. A small firm notices each person who joins it. We expect to notice this one first in the quality of our data.

Her work is valuation support. In practice that means the year-over-year reconciliation of census data: matching this year's member records to last year's, accounting for each new entrant, retirement, termination, and death, and catching the records that do not reconcile before they reach a valuation. It is careful work, and the firm's opinions rest on it. When the data show something, we want it written down as what the data show. When she has to make an assumption to fill a gap, we want that written down separately, with the reason for it. We use the plan document's own terms for each kind of event, and our workpapers should use them too.
A few practical points will make the first weeks easier. Most of them are habits, and habits are easiest to set at the start:

items: 1. Her first assignment is a reconciliation of a census the firm has already valued. She can compare her results with ours, and any difference is worth an hour with Jennifer Vasquez.

2. Census files contain personal information. They stay on the firm's systems and do not travel by ordinary email. Client data arrive through the secure file transfer site, and anything we send goes out the same way.
3. Nothing leaves the firm until a second person has checked it. That applies to a single exhibit as much as to a full report.
4. Questions about the work go to Jennifer Vasquez first. Early questions are welcome and cost nobody much time.
5. The firm supports study for actuarial exams. Study time is arranged with Jennifer Vasquez well ahead of a sitting, so the schedule can absorb it.

blocks.text: Within her first few months we expect Jennifer Johnson to run a census reconciliation from start to finish, with Jennifer Vasquez reviewing the result instead of directing each step. After that the work will widen to the other checks a valuation depends on. Recorded for the personnel file by Robert Lawrence, Managing Actuary.

Amanda White joins the consulting group

This is the onboarding record for Amanda White, who has joined the firm as an Actuarial Associate. Robert Lawrence prepared it for the personnel file, and it doubles as our welcome. We are pleased to have her with us, and we hope her first weeks here are orderly ones.

Amanda sits in the consulting group. She reports to Jennifer Vasquez, Consulting Actuary, who sets her assignments and reviews her work. Her work is exhibits and calculation checks for the reports we prepare for pension boards and fund trustees. A board reads the exhibits more closely than any other part of a report, and the exhibits are what counsel will quote. Every figure in them has to tie to the valuation output. Every figure also has to be labeled for what it is: measured from the data, or the result of an assumption. A reader should never have to guess which.

The first month is mostly reading and checking, which is how everyone here starts. Her sessions with Jennifer Vasquez will be weekly at first and less frequent as her checks need fewer corrections. Five habits will help from the beginning:

items: 1. Read several of the firm's signed reports in full before preparing an exhibit, so the house format and labeling are familiar.
2. Use the firm's exhibit templates as they stand. A template is changed once, for every report, and never inside a single report.
3. Correct a figure in the workpapers, not in the report. A number is fixed at its source and carried forward from there.
4. Keep a log of every discrepancy found, however small, and how it was resolved. The reviewer will ask for it.
5. Client data, including member census files, stay on the firm's systems and travel only through the secure file transfer site.

blocks.text: We do not expect independent judgments in the first months, and none goes into a client document until it has been reviewed. We do expect questions. Amanda should bring them to Jennifer Vasquez, or to whoever prepared the work she is checking, as soon as they arise. By the end of her first quarter we expect her to prepare a full set of exhibits for a valuation report, ready for review.

I am out all day next Tuesday for my exam, so I would like to trade phone coverage with you. You would take my Tuesday morning, and I would take your Thursday afternoon. Meridian Actuarial Advisors LLC

This overview is written for the boards, trustees, and company officers who are deciding whether to engage us, and for the counsel and staff who advise them. It describes what we do, how an assignment runs, and some of the work we have completed.
Our practice

We are consulting actuaries. We measure obligations that run for decades: retirement benefits owed by public systems and multiemployer funds, and the reserves a life insurer holds for its policyholders. Our clients use that work to set contributions, to report to regulators and auditors, and to make decisions about benefits and pricing. Those decisions are theirs. Our part is to tell them, as precisely as the data allow, where they stand and what the measurement depends on.

We have added consulting staff as the work has grown. We have kept one arrangement fixed while doing so: the actuary who scopes an assignment reviews it before it goes out, and the opinion is signed by the person who answers for it.
What we are engaged to do
Our services fall under four headings.

items: 1. Public retirement systems: funding valuations, accounting reports under GASB Statements No. 67 and No. 68, experience studies, and the assessment of risk that ASOP No. 51 now asks of pension actuaries.
2. Multiemployer funds: valuations for the trustees, the annual zone certification, and projections in support of a rehabilitation plan or a funding improvement plan.

3. Life insurers: reserve valuation, asset adequacy analysis, support for the appointed actuary's opinion and memorandum, and principle-based reserves under VM-20 as the transition period draws to a close.
4. Reviews: a second opinion on another actuary's valuation or assumptions, prepared for a board or its counsel.

How an assignment runs
The shape of an assignment changes little from one client to the next. A client can expect the following.

items: 1. An engagement letter before any work begins, stating the scope, the measurement date, the standards that apply, and the basis of the fee.
2. A data request that explains why each item is needed. We review what arrives for reasonableness and consistency, and we tell the client in writing about anything we could not reconcile.
3. A draft report for the client's review. It separates what the data show, what we assumed, and what we conclude, so that each can be questioned on its own.
4. A final report and opinion signed by Robert Lawrence, with its reliances and limitations set out in full.

blocks.text: Standards

Our work is performed under the Actuarial Standards of Practice. Several of them shape every report we issue: ASOP No. 23 on data quality, ASOP No. 41 on actuarial communications, and, for pension work, ASOP No. 4 and the standards on selecting economic and demographic assumptions. Where we rely on another party, such as a plan's auditor or an investment consultant's capital market assumptions, the report says so. It also says what we did to satisfy ourselves that the reliance was reasonable.

When a standard changes, we tell clients ahead of time how the change will affect what they receive. ASOP No. 51 is the recent case. Our pension reports now include a section on the risks that could make future results differ from the measurement, and on what those differences could mean for contributions. The section is written for the board, not for other actuaries.
Talking to us about an assignment

Robert Lawrence, Managing Actuary, is responsible for the firm's actuarial opinions and is the first contact for a new assignment. We usually begin with a conversation about the question the client is trying to answer. A written proposal follows. It sets out our understanding of that question before it says anything about method or fee, so that a misunderstanding can be caught while it is still cheap to correct.
